subject: maths
title: KS1 Maths diagnostic
curriculum: National Curriculum in England, key stage 1 mathematics programme of study (2013)
intro: Your tutor will read each question with you. Take your time and have a go at every question.

skills.name: Number and place value
skills.why: Knowing how numbers are built from tens and ones is the base for all adding and subtracting.
skills.strong: {name} counts, reads and compares numbers confidently and understands tens and ones.
skills.developing: {name} counts and reads numbers well but is less sure about tens and ones in bigger numbers.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet secure with tens and ones. Adding and subtracting depend on this, so it is the first thing to build.
skills.next_step: We will use counting, number lines and tens-and-ones games to make place value feel solid.

skills.name: Adding and subtracting
skills.why: Quick, confident adding and subtracting is used in almost every maths lesson from Year 1 onwards.
skills.strong: {name} adds and subtracts confidently, including with two-digit numbers.
skills.developing: {name} adds and subtracts small numbers well but finds two-digit numbers and missing numbers harder.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet confident adding and subtracting. This is used in almost every maths lesson, so it is worth real focus now.
skills.next_step: We will build number bonds and mental strategies with short, playful practice.

skills.name: Multiplying, dividing and fractions
skills.why: Counting in groups and sharing lead on to times tables, and halves and quarters are the first step into fractions.
skills.strong: {name} understands equal groups and sharing, and finds halves and quarters well.
skills.developing: {name} can count in 2s, 5s and 10s but is less sure sharing equally or finding a fraction of an amount.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet confident with groups, sharing and halves. Times tables in Year 3 build on this, so it is worth starting now.
skills.next_step: We will use objects and pictures to make grouping, sharing and halving make sense.

skills.name: Money, time and shape
skills.why: Money, time and shape are the maths children use every day, and they come up in every year of school.
skills.strong: {name} is confident with money, telling the time and the properties of shapes.
skills.developing: {name} knows the common shapes but finds telling the time or working with money harder.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet confident with money, time and shape. These come up in everyday life as well as in class, so they are worth practising.
skills.next_step: We will practise with real coins, clocks and shapes so these skills stick.

questions.explain: Counting on one from 19 crosses the tens boundary to 20. Watch for '110' or '100', which show the child is not yet secure crossing a ten.
4 + 3 = 7. Counting on from 4 (5, 6, 7) is fine; recalling it as a fact is better.

questions.ref: Y1: recognise and name common 2-D shapes
questions.stem: How many sides does a triangle have?
questions.explain: A triangle has 3 straight sides. 4 is a square or rectangle.

questions.ref: Y1: count in multiples of 2, 5 and 10
questions.stem:
Count in 2s: 2, 4, 6, 8, ...

What number comes next?
questions.explain: Counting in 2s: 8 + 2 = 10. An answer of 9 means the child counted on in ones.

questions.ref: Y1: identify more and less; Y2: compare numbers to 100
questions.explain: 31 has 3 tens, more than any other. Choosing 29 means the child looked at the 9 ones instead of the tens.

questions.ref: Y1: subtract one-digit and two-digit numbers to 20
questions.explain: 10 − 6 = 4, from the number bond 6 + 4 = 10. An answer of 16 means the child added.

questions.ref: Y1: recognise and know the value of coins
questions.stem: Which coins add up to exactly 10p?
questions.explain: 5p + 5p = 10p. The others make 9p, 6p and 8p. Counting coins rather than adding their values gives wrong answers here.

questions.ref: Y1: recognise, find and name a half
questions.explain: 8 shared into 2 equal groups is 4. 16 is double, not half. 2 comes from confusing half with 'share into 4'.

questions.ref: Y2: recognise the place value of each digit in a two-digit number
questions.stem: In the number 46, what does the 4 stand for?
questions.explain: The 4 is in the tens place, so it is worth 4 tens, which is 40. '4 ones' means the child reads digits without their place.

questions.ref: Y1: solve missing number problems such as 7 = ? − 9
questions.stem:
7 + ☐ = 15

What number goes in the box?
questions.explain: 15 − 7 = 8. An answer of 22 means the child added the two numbers they could see.

questions.ref: Y1: tell the time to the hour
questions.stem:
On a clock, the long minute hand points to 12 and the short hour hand points to 3.

What time is it?
questions.explain: The minute hand on 12 means 'o'clock', and the hour hand on 3 gives 3 o'clock. '12 o'clock' and 'quarter past 12' mix up the two hands.

questions.ref: Y2: solve problems involving multiplication, using arrays and repeated addition
questions.stem:
There are 5 bags. Each bag has 2 apples in it.

How many apples are there altogether?
questions.explain: 5 groups of 2 is 5 × 2 = 10. An answer of 7 means the child added 5 and 2.

questions.ref: Y2: compare and order numbers from 0 up to 100; use <, > and = signs
questions.explain: 54 is greater than 45, so the sign is >. Choosing '=' means the child thinks the same digits make the same number.

questions.ref: Y2: add a two-digit number and a two-digit number
questions.stem:
Sam has 38 stickers. He is given 25 more.

How many stickers does he have now?
questions.explain: 38 + 25 = 63 (30 + 20 = 50, 8 + 5 = 13, 50 + 13 = 63). An answer of 53 means the extra ten from 8 + 5 was lost.

questions.ref: Y2: find 1/3, 1/4, 2/4 and 3/4 of a set of objects or quantity
questions.explain: 12 shared into 4 equal groups is 3. 4 comes from confusing 'a quarter' with the number 4, 6 is a half, and 48 is 12 × 4.

questions.ref: Y2: solve simple problems involving money, including giving change
questions.stem:
Mia has 50p. She spends 35p on a pencil.

How much change does she get?
questions.explain: 50p − 35p = 15p. Counting on from 35 to 50 works well: 5p to 40, then 10p to 50. An answer of 85 means the child added.
